output.best_reason: Version B has the most distinct voice: Madame Monnier is dry, guarded and quick, with lines like "he gave the guests their lesson" and "You may write that down." Her answers carry the facts (the watch, the quarrel, the debt to Girard, the cigars, the clock) inside characterization, and the tension builds through small evasions, such as her refusal to weep and her "it is the only way I have ever won" about not looking at the clock. Its period texture comes from concrete details (thirty-one years of marriage, the repeater, Chopin) without archaic pastiche. Version E ranks next: its closing lines ("The doctor will want to go home, and so, I think, will Félix") and the cigar detail give it real menace, though its formal address is repeated a little heavily. Version D is strong on voice, but its opening household roll call reads like a recited list. Version A is competent and clean but flatter, with the facts coming in more of a sequence. Version C has good lines ("I poured the wine") but leans on overwrought metaphors about friendship and marriage wearing smooth, and it drops the tension the others keep alive.
